title: Evolution of Concepts in Language Model Pre-Training
one_liner: By watching what patterns the model learns to recognize during training, we can see that learning happens in two clear stages: first raw stats, then genuine concepts.
lead: When a language model trains on text, its internal wiring changes dramatically. But how? This paper watches the model learn by taking snapshots at different training steps and identifying what patterns (called features) the model recognizes at each moment. The key finding: learning splits into two phases. Early on, the model just memorizes basic statistics about word counts and sequences. Then suddenly, around step 1,000 of training, real concepts emerge—patterns like subject-verb agreement or induction—that directly enable downstream tasks because these patterns are specific, reusable rules that apply reliably to new examples, unlike memorized statistics which capture only aggregate frequencies.

paras: When engineers train a large language model, they feed it billions of words and watch the loss (the error score) drop. But the loss dropping tells you almost nothing about what the model is actually learning inside. Are all the learning steps the same? Do all concepts emerge together? Do early learning steps build toward later ones, or are they wasted effort? Nobody knows—it is a complete black box.

If you try the naive approach—just reading the numbers and weights after training is done—you get a soup. The weights are tangled together, storing thousands of overlapping patterns at once. You cannot see which patterns the model recognizes at step 10 versus step 10,000, or whether an early pattern is later discarded or refined. You are blind to the actual learning journey.

callout.html: The paper watches the model learn by tracking which interpretable patterns (features) it recognizes at each training checkpoint, revealing a hidden two-stage structure beneath the loss curve.

panels.title: 1. The problem: loss drops but why?
panels.caption: Training loss falls smoothly, yet we see no window into what the model learns.

panels.title: 2. Early training: random initialization
panels.caption: At step 0, weights are random noise. Some random patterns happen to activate.

panels.title: 3. Surprise: features vanish then reappear
panels.caption: Around step 1,000, old random patterns collapse; real concepts suddenly form and stick.

panels.title: 4. Complex patterns emerge later
panels.caption: Simple patterns like word order appear at step 1,000. Reasoning patterns grow until step 100,000.

panels.title: 5. Causal proof: remove features, break tasks
panels.caption: Remove one learned concept, and downstream tasks fail. Features cause performance gains.

steps.text: Save the model's internal activations (lists of numbers flowing through the network) at 32 different training steps, from the start to step 143,000.

A sparse autoencoder (a small auxiliary network) tries to reconstruct each snapshot's activations using a combination of named sparse features, like a decoder finding the minimum set of concepts needed to explain what the network computed.
For each named feature, plot when it first becomes active. Most features are born around step 1,000; a few emerge much later (step 100,000).
Use an LLM to score each feature's learned patterns (simple or rich). Early features are shallow (word order); later features are deep (induction, subject-verb agreement).
Run a circuit test: when you silence one learned feature, does a downstream task (like recognizing a verb matching its subject) break? If yes, the feature caused the performance gain.

paras: The paper does not change the model itself or its training. Instead, it changes what we observe: from a single global loss number to a detailed map of when each interpretable pattern (feature) emerges during training.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: feature emergence step
hidden.name: When each pattern first activates
paras: During training, random weights gradually organize themselves into recognizable patterns. Each pattern—such as subject-verb agreement, or detecting the previous token—awakens at a specific moment. The emergence step is the training checkpoint where that pattern first becomes active and stays active (rather than flickering on and off). Some patterns spring to life at step 500; others wait until step 50,000. The paper measures emergence by watching the activation strength of each feature across all 32 snapshots and finding the first checkpoint where that feature consistently activates.

The paper estimates emergence by training a sparse autoencoder (a decoder network) on snapshots side by side. When the decoder is forced to compress each snapshot into the same set of named features, the ones that matter at step 10 are weak; the same features at step 1,000 are strong; and at step 500 they are flickering in between. The paper plots this strength over time and calls the step where strength first rises and sticks the emergence step.

heat.caption: Darker means the feature is more active (stronger encoding) at that training step. Most features are weak at step 0 and 100, hot by step 1,000.

reads.html: At the very start of training, the model has random weights and no real patterns. Around training step 1,000, many patterns suddenly activate strongly. Later (steps 10,000–100,000), richer, more specialized patterns emerge.

The paper uses crosscoders to decompose activations into sparse features and tracks decoder norm (the strength of each feature's encoding) across 32 snapshots spanning steps 0 to 143,000. Emergent features show a drastic rise in activation strength; initialization features (present at step 0) decay or vanish around step 128–1,000.

mechanism.h2: Why watching emergence reveals two stages
paras: The learning process has two hidden phases, and emergence timing exposes both. In the first phase (steps 0–1,000), the model is just memorizing basic statistics: what fraction of sentences have a noun, how often nouns come before verbs, what the letter frequencies are. These are not really concepts; they are just aggregate numbers from the data. Importantly, the model can shrink its loss dramatically using only statistics—loss falls from high to low without any real reasoning patterns forming. You can see this because the sparse autoencoder finds almost no features activating until step 1,000. The model is not yet recognizing specific, reusable patterns.

Then around step 1,000, something shifts. New patterns suddenly emerge. The model begins isolating specific recognizable concepts: this word is a verb, this position is the start of a clause, this sequence looks like an induction pattern (if A appears once here and again there, C probably comes next). These are actual concepts, not just stats, because they are built from combinations of input tokens and can be applied to new examples. The paper calls this the feature learning phase. The loss still falls (because loss was already pretty low from memorized stats), but now it is refinement: the model tunes up these concepts over the next 100,000 steps, getting them precise and general. By tracking emergence, you can see this two-stage structure in the data itself.

stages.s: Sparse autoencoder decomposes activations into named features
Plot each feature's activation strength over time
Identify emergence step: where each feature's strength first rises and sticks
Timeline showing two phases: stats only until 1,000, then concepts emerge

math.words: Total loss is reconstruction error plus a penalty for complexity. Reconstruction error: how far off the decoder's guess is from the real activations. Complexity penalty: how many features did the decoder actually turn on to make that guess.
math.equation: L = sum_snapshots || activations - reconstructed || squared + lambda × sum_snapshots sum_features (feature_activation × feature_norm)
symbols: the real numbers flowing through the model layer at this snapshot
the decoder's approximation using sparse features
how much this feature is on (0 or a small number)
the magnitude (strength) of this feature's decoder weights
the knob that trades off accuracy versus simplicity (higher pushes sparser)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Snapshot at step 100: real activations are [2.3, -1.1, 0.8]. Decoder uses feature A (norm 1.2) and feature C (norm 0.9), producing [2.4, -1.0, 0.7].
Sparsity: feature A is on (activation = 1), feature C is on (activation = 1), all others off. Cost = lambda * (1*1.2 + 1*0.9 + 0*0 + ...) = lambda * 2.1.
Total loss = 0.03 + lambda * 2.1. If lambda is high, the decoder is forced to use fewer features. If lambda is low, accuracy wins. At each snapshot, the decoder rebalances.

math.note: The sparse decoder is forced to pick a small set of features to reconstruct each snapshot; by comparing decoded feature sets across snapshots, we see which features are 'on' early, which turn on at step 1,000, and which wake up later.

bars.h2: Comparison of what is learned when

charts.title: Early stage (steps 0–1,000): statistics dominate
charts.note: The model shrinks loss using only statistics and token-order statistics. Real concepts have not emerged yet.

charts.title: Late stage (steps 1,000–100,000): concepts refine
charts.note: Same statistics, plus new concept patterns emerging. Loss barely improves because it was already near the information-theoretic minimum (the entropy of natural text), so further shrinkage is impossible; instead, the model trades remaining capacity for more precise, generalizable patterns, which is why concept fidelity soars.

items.html: If the sparsity knob (lambda) is too high, the decoder is forced to be so sparse it misses real features. If it is too low, the decoder spreads features too thin and cannot detect clean emergence steps. The paper uses ablation (trying many values) to find the right balance, but other work might not.

The paper uses 32 snapshots, chosen to oversample early steps (all 20 before step 10,000) and undersample late steps. If the real emergence happens at step 8,000 but you only have snapshots at 0, 2000, and 15000, you miss it. The choice of snapshots shapes which emergences you see.

items.b: Features are tools, not ground truth.
items.html: The sparse autoencoder finds features that are linear combinations (sums and differences) of the actual neural activations. A 'real' concept in the model might not compress into a linear feature, or might require several features. The emergence step measures when the decoder's chosen features activate, not when the concept is fully learned internally.

Use a well-tuned sparse autoencoder, oversample early checkpoints to catch phase transitions, and validate emergence steps by checking that silencing those features breaks downstream tasks. This is what the paper does.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Pick a small language model (e.g., GPT-2 or Pythia-70M). Save activations at 10 training steps: 0, 100, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000, 100000. Train a sparse autoencoder on all 10 snapshots at once (using the same set of features for all). Plot the activation strength (decoder norm or mean feature magnitude) for each feature at each step. You should see most feature strengths stay near zero until step 500–1000, then spike and stay high. A few features (initialization artifacts) should spike early then crash. This plot is visual proof of the two-stage process.
demo.metric_eq: emergence_step = first_checkpoint where feature_strength > threshold and stays > threshold thereafter; two_stage_clarity = (step_1000_feature_count - step_500_feature_count) / step_1000_feature_count; should be > 0.6
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss the phase transition: a dense cluster of features emerging around step 1,000, preceded by silence and followed by refinement.
